REI and Dick’s are two of the names that come up the most often, and they handle the holiday very differently. REI is again giving its employees a paid day off on Friday, November 27, so its deals land early. Dick’s has typically stretched its sale across the weekend. Think Hoka, Asics, and Brooks top trainers with discounts of $50 or more, with deeper discounts on previous years’ models. The deals don’t match model to model, and each outlet has different shoes at different prices. For example, REI offers steeper discounts on Hoka, and Dick’s has better pricing on brands like Adidas.
The Hoka Bondi 9 is a favorite among distance runners, especially those with flatter feet. It has a supercritical foam midsole that makes it light and responsive, with a snug fit, a generously padded collar, and comfortable, max-stack cushioning. It’s a big improvement over the Bondis of antiquity, and it’s one of their most popular shoes overall. And the price difference between REI and Dick’s is significant, with REI the clear winner.

Your race bib can tell organizers a lot more than how quickly you finished. At Spain's 61st edition of Behobia–San Sebastián, it also helped them figure out whether you started when you were supposed to. As it turns out, getting a little too eager at the starting line can be enough to cost you an official result.
Organizers confirmed that 853 participants were disqualified from the November 8 event, a popular 20K race that attracted 27,172 runners this year. According to Spanish outlets Mundo Deportivo and 3Cat, starting in an earlier wave than assigned was a major reason behind the unusually high number.
The race sorts participants into groups based on their previous performances, with staggered start times designed to help manage the crowds. Runners can move back to a later wave if they wish, but jumping ahead to an earlier one is grounds for disqualification. It's a rule that should sound familiar to anyone who's run a race with NYRR, as they follow the same policy and warn that moving into a faster wave or corral can cost runners their results.
With thousands of people lining up, slipping into an earlier group can go unnoticed, but timing chips attached to race bibs allow organizers to track when participants cross the starting line and other checkpoints along the course.
Other violations, including using another runner's bib without an authorized transfer, are against the rules and can also result in disqualification. However, organizers haven't provided explanations for every case, making it unclear how many involved starting-wave violations.
According to figures released by organizers, 29,301 people registered for the event, and 26,947 crossed the 12.4-mile course’s finish line in San Sebastián. Of those who completed the race, a little more than 3 percent were disqualified.
While it sounds like a lot, 853 is actually an improvement compared to previous years. In 2023, a whopping 1,327 runners were disqualified, followed by 958 in 2024 and 918 last year. So the numbers are heading in the right direction, although there's clearly still some confusion—or disregard—when it comes to following the pre-start rules.
Runner’s World has contacted race organizers for details about the disqualifications, including whether affected participants have an opportunity to appeal.

Quantum Computing’s Investment Problem Is Becoming Clearer
The quantum computing industry is confronting a distinction between technological progress and commercial profitability. Processors are improving, yet recent results suggest that useful systems are advancing faster than sustainable business models. This raises an investment question: will the developers of quantum processors capture the largest profits, or will established semiconductor and computing companies benefit more from the infrastructure needed to make quantum computing practical?
The latest earnings provide a useful test. D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) reported just $4.5 million in third-quarter revenue despite substantial nine-month bookings growth. Rigetti Computing (RGTI) reported a 28% revenue decline to $1.4 million. IonQ (IONQ | IONQ Price Prediction) reported $173.8 million in revenue, but nearly half came from acquired SkyWater foundry operations. These are materially different forms of commercialization.
Meanwhile, IBM (IBM) is deploying integrated quantum systems, Intel (INTC) is pursuing silicon spin qubits and quantum software, and Nvidia (NVDA) is positioning its accelerated computing infrastructure to support multiple quantum architectures. Their financial exposure differs fundamentally from that of the pure plays.
According to Table 1, the four pure-play stocks declined between 41.05% and 64.54% during the one-year period ending November 10, 2026. The separate all-time-high measure is more dramatic: Quantum Computing Inc. was 98.63% below its reported historical peak. That unusually large historical drawdown may be affected by corporate-action adjustments and should not be confused with its one-year return.
These declines do not prove quantum computing is failing. They show investors are revising what they are willing to pay today for revenue and profits that may be years away. The most useful comparison is therefore not qubit counts alone, but the pace at which each company converts technological advances into recognized sales and improving operating economics.

Apple (AAPL) and Seagate Technology (STX) are both owned on the bet that AI lifts demand for their hardware. Apple management sees AI as a reason for customers to upgrade. Data center customers, meanwhile, took 90% of the capacity Seagate shipped in the September quarter. That makes Seagate look like the more direct way to own the bet, if those buyers keep ordering at higher prices. So how much of Seagate’s supply have those customers already claimed?
Seagate Has Committed Most Of Its Supply Through 2028
Seagate’s data center customers signed up for years, not one quarter at a time. On Seagate’s October 27, 2026 call, management said long-term supply agreements through calendar 2028 allocate the vast majority of the capacity the company can supply to data centers. In the nearer term, Seagate expects December quarter revenue of $4.8 billion, plus or minus $100 million, following $4.2 billion in the September quarter. Prices for 2028 are not set yet.
Apple expects December quarter revenue to grow 7% to 10% from a year earlier, following 12% growth in the September quarter, and gave no outlook beyond December. That range reflects constrained supply. Apple expects to be short of memory for Mac and iPad because demand has been higher than it expected. So Seagate’s demand is signed up years ahead, while Apple’s outlook covers one quarter and is limited by supply, mainly of memory.
Is Seagate Raising Prices Faster Than Costs?
So far, Seagate is. The company recorded an operating margin of 48.9% in fiscal Q1 2027, the quarter ended October 2, 2026, against 26.9% in the same quarter a year earlier. Management said better pricing and product mix more than offset higher costs for some outside parts, though passing those costs on is sometimes not so predictable. Seagate’s spending is light too. Management expects capital spending of 4% to 6% of revenue in fiscal 2027, and Seagate expects to hold more cash than debt by the end of calendar 2026.
Like Seagate, Apple is paying more for a part it buys: memory. Apple’s gross margin was 47.9% in the September quarter, and management expects 45% to 46% in the December quarter, with most of the drop coming from higher memory costs. Apple raised prices on Mac and iPad in June and on iPhone in September to offset part of those costs.

What Should Snap Stock Holders Take From Its Third-Quarter Report?
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
Snap (SNAP) stock fell 14.0% in the session after the company reported its Q3 FY2026 results on November 4, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 4.4%. Earnings per share beat analysts’ estimates, but revenue fell short, and revenue is the line shareholders should look at first. So where did Snap’s sales come up short?
Snap’s Sales Shortfall Was In Advertising
Advertising accounts for most of what Snap sells, and those sales grew just 4% from a year earlier in Q3 FY2026, management said on the November 4 call. Other revenue grew 84%, led by the Snapchat+, Memories Storage and Lens+ subscriptions. Total revenue came to $1.72 billion, landing 2.4% below the analysts’ consensus, though inside the range management had guided. Earnings per share were $0.19, against a consensus of $0.16. That figure is on a different measure from the reported profit given below. Daily active users grew to 495 million, which also fell short of analysts’ estimates.
Inside the advertising business, the two kinds of ads diverged. Management said direct response ads, which are aimed at purchases, grew strongly, while brand advertising, which is aimed at awareness, declined year-over-year and weighed on Snap’s overall growth. Snap’s shares fell further than its peers in the same session: Pinterest lost 6.7% and Meta Platforms lost 4.0%.
Is Snap’s Revenue Growth Slowing?
Snap’s revenue growth slowed from the quarter before, but stayed above its pace of a year earlier. Revenue rose 14.3% from a year earlier in Q3 FY2026, against 9.8% growth in Q3 FY2025. Growth had reached 18.9% in Q2 FY2026. Management said that earlier quarter benefited from easier comparisons on World Cup-related spending.
For Q4 FY2026, management guided revenue to a range of $1.950 billion to $1.985 billion. That would be 13.6% to 15.7% more than Snap reported for the same quarter a year earlier. The growth range includes Snap’s Q3 growth rate, so management expects growth to stay near its Q3 pace rather than return to the Q2 rate.
Snap’s profit improved even as growth slowed. The company earned $56.5 million in Q3 FY2026, against a loss of $104 million a year earlier, and management said its total cost structure grew just 1% year-over-year. Over the past twelve months, Snap still lost $151 million.
What Did Snap’s Management Say About Brand Ads?
Management said brand advertising declined mainly because of lower spending by consumer packaged goods companies, driven by macro pressures in the U.S. and the Middle East. Management pointed to growth from other industries, such as financial services in the U.S., and said it was seeing a bit of acceleration on the ad side in Q4 FY2026.
Management also said direct response ads keep growing as a share of Snap’s business, which it expects to continue in the short term, and that improvements in its brand products and sales approach should kick in as Snap moves into 2027. Both are management’s expectations, not results yet.
Snap’s quarter showed its profit improving while its advertising barely grew. Advertising revenue growth is the figure to watch when Snap reports its Q4 FY2026 results, expected in February 2027.

Maryland’s highest court heard arguments on an appeal Monday that will affect 1,300 lawsuits filed under the Child Victims Act.
The 2023 law effectively eliminated time barriers for someone to file a court claim of institutional sex abuse. At issue are the roughly 1,300 cases in which the alleged sexual assaults took place before 1982, a time when the state had absolute immunity from lawsuits. The Supreme Court of Maryland is being asked to decide if the General Assembly, when it passed the landmark 2023 law, clearly and knowingly waived that immunity.
The article is republished from Maryland Matters.
Jonathan Massey, attorney for a plaintiff known only as J.C., said the waiver of damage caps in the 2023 law are proof of the legislature’s intent.
The change “is the waiver of state sovereign immunity, and make changes that assume there will be a damages cap, assuming there will be liability to the state, right? That’s why you need a damages cap because there’s going to be liability to the state. I don’t think the legislature was silent in 2023 on the issue of sovereign immunity,” Massey said during oral arguments.
Monday’s appeal involves a claim of sexual abuse from 1977, when J.C. was a patient at the old Prince George’s Hospital Center, where she claimed a doctor molested her during a stay there.
Lawyers for the state argued that the state at the time was protected by sovereign immunity. Prior to 1982, the state could not face civil lawsuits, and the state’s lawyers asked a Prince George’s County judge to dismiss the case on those grounds.
Attorneys representing the state filed roughly 200 motions to dismiss cases involving claims before July 1, 1982. The state has argued that the legislature must expressly waive the 40-year old immunity provision, something they said the 2023 law did not do.
Judges at the Circuit Court level granted four motions at the time the appeal was filed with the state’s highest court.
The Prince George’s County court denied the state’s motion without a hearing or explanation. But judges in Frederick County and Baltimore City have agreed with the state. Each dismissed cases under the sovereign immunity argument.
The Supreme Court’s ruling on the issue comes with a dollar sign attached.
Cases involving allegations occurring before 1982 comprise about 11% of the 12,000 cases that have been filed under the Child Victims Act. The 2023 law capped damages against the state at $890,000 per occurrence, but the definition of an “occurrence” is still being debated.
The full extent of the state’s potential liability has never been publicly stated. A rough estimate shows potentially budget-busting consequences.
If each plaintiff alleged just one occurrence and received the maximum award, the potential liability to the state could be about $11 billion. That estimate is nearly four times the structural budget gap projected for the fiscal 2028 budget to be introduced in January.
The potential payout could go up if a court or jury defines “occurrence” as each instance of abuse, rather than bundling instances based on any number of related circumstances. Settlements could reduce the potential liability.
If lawyers for the state are successful in getting the pre-1982 cases blocked, it would reduce the state’s potential liability by “more than a billion dollars,” the Office of the Attorney General argued in a filing earlier this year.

I don’t know about you, but I have days, weeks, and months when my running is challenging.
Sometimes that challenge arises when you’re coming back from an injury or an offseason, while other times it can be due to particularly busy or stressful times in life. When that time comes, even getting out the door feels daunting. When that’s the case, a little nudge can go a long way to getting back on track.
I find that this one small promise can help me quickly return to real running: 7×7.
No fewer than four times so far this decade, I’ve gone to my tried-and-true crutch: I run seven miles a day for seven straight days. It’s a small idea, but it’s worked every time.
Every one of those times, I was in a place where even the first seven-mile run felt daunting, but I told myself I was going to do it. I got out the door, and then again the next day, and the day after that, until I’d completed seven days. If I had to walk the second half of the week, that’s fine. If I was slow as all get out, it didn’t matter. The point was to get out there and cover the ground.
After I completed that commitment, I’d gotten over that hump, that activation energy, that dark hill that stood in front of me, I found myself on a ridge I could run along. I’d renewed a habit. I could run for an hour. That was fine. If I could run for an hour every day for a week — no matter how I felt, how tired I was, or what the weather was — then I could run for an hour on any day that followed.
And while 7×7 itself was a small commitment, it actually stood in lieu of a larger one hiding behind it, and that was a recommitment to myself as a runner. It helped me re-identify as a runner and prioritize that time in my daily life.
Now, 7×7 might not be a magical commitment for you, but I bet you can find ways to jump-start your own running if you need to. Here are some thoughts on how you might do that successfully.
- Keep it short. If you’re having a rough patch in your running, it might be too much to commit to running every day for a year. But it could be five days, two weeks, every day during a vacation, or whatever timeframe works for you.
- Keep the bar low (enough). If you’re trying to overcome a hill, don’t make your challenge a mountain. While seven miles of running might seem daunting to me on the first day of 7×7, I know from decades of running that an hour is totally doable, even if it’s double what I might run during a slump. For me, even upping that to 10 miles a day might go from restarting a good habit to physically challenging.
- Make it concrete. Have numbers. If it’s going to be running a certain number of days, or if it’s a certain number of miles in a week, whatever it is, establish a concrete goal because you hit it or you don’t.
- Bonus: Keep it a little lighthearted. I wish I had a game or an explicitly fun aspect to 7×7, but the name by itself will have to be lighthearted enough. Surely you can create something more lighthearted than I have.

Cardinals president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom is entering his second offseason as the head executive for a St. Louis club that finished 77-85 in 2026.
Bloom spoke to the media during the General Managers Meetings at the Aria Resort and Casino in Las Vegas on Tuesday to recount the 2026 season and look ahead. Just as with every other team and its baseball executives, there’s a bit more urgency than usual at this time of the year, with the Collective Bargaining Agreement set to expire on Dec. 1, meaning there will likely be more free-agent and trade activity during this month than most years.
Bloom, however, is seemingly more concerned with the overall picture for the Cardinals and trying to address areas across the entire organization.
“Certainly for us, we’re working on our staff. We're working to talk to agents about their players and free agency,” Bloom said. “We're working to talk to other teams. So there's really three fronts we're operating on.”
Asked by reporters if there was any urgency about fixing the roster and coaching staff before Dec. 1, Bloom didn’t necessarily seem rushed by the upcoming deadline.
“A lot of these things are just things that you want to be out in front of as much as you can,” Bloom said. “So at least for us, it hasn't really changed much.”
Bloom’s Cardinals showed a lot of promise in his first full season at the helm, given that the club traded major players from the previous rosters last offseason, including Willson Contreras, Sonny Gray and Nolan Arenado. The breakouts from JJ Wetherholt, who finished third in NL Rookie of the Year voting in 2026, and Jordan Walker and the continued development from the likes of Alec Burleson, Andre Pallante and Michael McGreevy have only added optimism for 2027 and beyond.
Now comes the task of supplementing a roster that flirted with an NL Wild Card spot, whether via free agency and trades or a rapidly improving farm system.
“I think we need to do a lot more things that are consistent with what we started doing last year to keep going, to keep integrating other players, keep pushing to get the most out of things, keep looking to acquire more pieces for the core and then to put the right pieces around,” Bloom said.
That next wave of young Cardinals talent could take on an even more pronounced role in 2027. Beyond the aforementioned players, youngsters like Joshua Báez and Leo Bernal, who already showed promise in the Majors, while top prospects Rainiel Rodriguez (MLB Pipeline’s No. 1 Cardinals prospect) and Liam Doyle (No. 2 prospect) figure to be impact talents soon.
“There's a couple different angles that we can look at. One is making sure -- whether they’re players that have already debuted with us or players that hopefully that debut is in the relatively near future -- making sure we have lanes for them,” Bloom said. “We don't want to hand them anything, but we want to make sure we have lanes for them to break in, and if they have broken in, to be able to thrive.”
That other lane is looking via free agency and trade to supplement this growing list of young Cardinals that could form the next great St. Louis team.
“There's also looking outside the organization from a trade standpoint as to whether there are players who might be able to join that core for the long haul, whether in a front-and-center role or a supporting role,” Bloom said. “That's really important, too. States are counting on battery farms. Some towns don’t want them.
A battery storage facility sits in front of wind turbines near Palm Springs, California. States and utilities are building battery farms but many communities oppose them. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)
SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition.
The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities.
The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power.
But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them.
Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future.
‘Meteoric growth’
Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles.
At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants.
“The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.”
Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances.
With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand.

Much of the midterm “blue tsunami” came from diverse, enthusiastic young voters with financial struggles who flocked to the polls, and also Trump voters sitting out the election, according to two experts analyzing turnout in a handful of states with detailed results.
The results, they say, could mean a mandate for bringing costs down and more power for young Latinos, but also a danger for Democrats if Republicans rally back to the polls in 2028.
“It looks like more Trump voters who didn’t vote Republican stayed home rather than switching (to Democrats),” said Lenny Bronner, founder of Broome Street Labs and a data scientist formerly with the Washington Post, based on his analysis of 13 states with detailed results.
“Those voters are easier for the GOP to win back than those who chose a Democratic candidate,” Bronner said.
Bronner estimated 75% of Democratic gains came from a turnout gap and about 20% from Republicans switching sides and voting for Democrats.
His analysis included turnout data for Texas, Georgia, South Carolina, Colorado, New Mexico, Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas, Iowa, Florida, West Virginia, Minnesota and Michigan. The share of Democrats’ gain that came from a turnout gap ranged from 40% for Texas to 133% for Michigan among the states he studied; some states had only partial detailed results.
Bronner wrote on X (formerly Twitter) that partial results in Texas showed that voters flipped their ballots more than expected; 45% of Democratic gains there came from voters switching away from Republicans. “So far, Texas is the only state where our model indicates that persuasion explains more of Democrats net gain than turnout does!” he wrote.
A University of Florida political science professor, Michael McDonald, also saw a turnout surge for young voters faced with high grocery bills, student loan debt and sluggish wages, based on detailed results from Georgia and Colorado. Trump’s older voter constituency was more likely to stay home, he wrote in a Substack post.
In both Colorado and Georgia, 18- to 25-year-olds had the biggest jump in turnout compared with the 2022 midterms, he wrote, while it fell for voters older than 40.

The swirl of sex-and-spying allegations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom?
Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system.
Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector.
A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion.
But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said.
"Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said.
Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But with Huang under scrutiny by the FBI, Congress, and Nvidia's board over his relationship with a woman who The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, analysts see a wide range of outcomes as suddenly possible, including the potential removal of Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993.

Its stock recovered Wednesday, rising more than 4% as of midday. What you do to recover between runs matters just as much as the miles themselves. But knowing what your body needs isn’t always straightforward. Should you head out for an easy run or take the day off? Is that soreness normal, or a sign of an injury about to derail everything? And which recovery tools are actually worth the hype?
This guide helps you navigate those decisions, starting with the fundamentals. Plus, we’ll help you choose a training plan to ease back into running after a race, your offseason, or an injury (both minor and burdensome).
Whether you’re bouncing back from a tough workout or gearing up for your next training block, start planning your recovery here.
Recovery Fundamentals
Recovery doesn’t have to be complicated, but it does require giving the basics as much attention as your workouts. Easy runs, rest days, postrun fueling, and sleep all help your body manage the work you’re putting in. That means keeping most of your miles at a pace where you can comfortably hold a conversation, rather than turning every run into another hard effort.

It also means taking at least one full day off from training each week—and more if you’re new to running or need extra recovery.
What you do after a run matters, too: Carbohydrates replenish energy stores, protein supports muscle repair, and sufficient sleep gives your body time to recover and rebuild.

- Toasted bagel with cream cheese, smoked salmon, and sliced pickled beets
- A bowl of cereal with milk
- Two hard-boiled eggs with a glass of tomato juice

Managing Soreness and Fatigue
Sore legs after a tough workout can come with the territory. But knowing when to take it easy—and when to stop running—isn’t always obvious. Before you push through discomfort, pay attention to how it feels, whether it’s improving, and how it affects the way you move.
Delayed-onset muscle soreness, or DOMS, typically develops within 24 to 72 hours after a challenging workout and gradually fades with time and movement. Here’s how to recognize normal soreness and spot signs that may indicate something more serious.
Typical muscle soreness tends to:
- Feel like a dull ache or stiffness
- Improve with stretching and recovery tools
- Dissipate after a few days
If your soreness isn’t affecting your day-to-day and you can move normally, a short, easy run may help ease the discomfort.
Signs of a possible injury include:
- Sharp or stabbing pain
- Pain that lasts longer than three days (even if it’s just when you’re running)
- Swelling or bruising
- Numbness, tingling, weakness, or feeling like a joint might give out
- Pain that interferes with your running gait and then eventually your walking gait
If you notice these warning signs, stop running and seek guidance from a healthcare professional rather than trying to push through.

To be at the frontier of quantum computing, industry-relevant applications demand both computational quality and speed. Speed matters because a quantum computer delivers its answer in samples: each run of a quantum circuit returns one result. Scale and quality enable increasingly complex computations, but speed determines whether these demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost.

When winter arrives, it’s tempting to put your running goals on hold until the temperatures warm up, the days get longer, and the roads clear. Cold temperatures make it harder to leave a warm bed, while snow and ice can turn a familiar route into a much slower—and more slippery—run.
For months at a time, Michelle Baxter’s running routes in Anchorage, Alaska, were covered in packed snow and ice. After a snowstorm, plows could take days to reach every neighborhood, and by then, cars had compressed the fallen snow onto the roads. Even after the plows came through, the slick surface often remained.
Baxter—now an RRCA- and V.02-certified run coach—spent 15 years living in Alaska and training through winters like these, figuring out how to keep running through harsh, unmotivating conditions.
She trained for 12 marathons in that time, continuing to build fitness year after year. Eventually, she even achieved her most ambitious running goal: breaking three hours in the marathon. After eight years of attempting to break the barrier—and a heartbreakingly close 3:01:14 at Humpy’s Marathon in Anchorage in August 2021—Baxter finally ran a 2:58:24 at the California International Marathon in December 2021. She has since lowered her PR to 2:56:57 at the Indianapolis Monumental Marathon.
Your winter running routes may not be covered in snow and ice for six months straight, but chances are you’ll face your own challenges as the temperature drops in the coming weeks and months. The good news: Baxter’s experience can help you navigate tough terrain and make the most of your training.
Here’s how you can put her lessons to work this winter so when the ice thaws, you’re ready to run your fastest race yet.
Find Gear That Makes Winter Running Manageable
What you wear can make or break a winter run, Baxter says. When you’re too cold, too warm, or worried about taking a spill around every tight corner, it’s hard to focus on any other aspect of the run. Baxter spent years figuring out what works, and her gear advice starts with two essentials: finding reliable footwear and appropriate layers for the conditions.
→Getting a Grip on Slippery Surfaces
In Anchorage, finding reliable footing was Baxter’s biggest winter challenge. She initially resisted buying studded shoes, assuming they wouldn’t make much difference. But once she tried them, she was surprised by how much more confident she felt in every step.
For packed snow, Baxter often wore regular trainers fitted with screws in the outsoles, which she added herself.
On sheer ice, Baxter preferred shoes made with built-in carbide studs; she swears by the Icebug brand. “You can wear these shoes and make a 90-degree turn and feel so confident running on ice—like sheer ice,” Baxter says. “They were a game-changer for me.”
You may not encounter sheets of ice on your regular running routes, but consider the conditions you encounter most often and look for an option suited to them.
Now living in Minnesota, Baxter says she reaches for studded shoes if she expects at least half of a run to cover potentially snowy or icy ground. She notes that while the shoes may be slightly less comfortable than your normal trainers, protecting your body from harm is the number-one priority during the winter months of training.
“I just think it’s worth it to feel confident running on the slippery surfaces and not risk injuring yourself,” she says.

At the top of the range, Anthropic would raise about $64.4 billion, and the shares would be worth about $916 billion to $1.02 trillion on a basic-share count.

In early afternoon trading on November 11, 2026, Amazon was down 1.32% at $267.29, and Alphabet was up 2.85% at $295.58. The filing does not explain either move.
How a 28-Day Window Becomes $81 Billion
To get run-rate revenue, Anthropic takes consumption fees from the trailing 28 days and multiplies them by 13. It then adds monthly subscription fees multiplied by 12. Because of that growth, one strong month can quickly push the reported figure up.
So the October jump is impressive, but it may not last. The filing says the figure does not replace GAAP revenue, is not a forecast, has not been independently verified, and can swing with holiday usage. It can also include amounts from customers later found violating usage policies.

NEW YORK and LONDON, Nov. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Navatar, a Salesforce-based CRM for private equity and M&A firms, today announced enhanced Salesforce Model Context Protocol (MCP) capabilities that bring relevant information buried in documents into Claude-assisted work, even when users don't know which document contains it. When professionals submit a prompt or start an activity, Navatar's MCP uses relevant document information alongside structured CRM data. Users don't have to find and open each source document first.
The capabilities cover supported documents stored in Navatar CRM, SharePoint, other connected document management systems, and shared drives. Document analysis is no longer a separate task. Document information becomes part of the context Claude uses as professionals research opportunities, review deals, and carry out supported actions in Claude or inside Navatar.
Professionals can still verify findings, select relevant information, and add it to the right CRM fields. Using document information to inform an activity does not mean every finding is automatically written into the firm's records.
Users Shouldn't Have to Know Where to Look
In private equity and M&A, important deal and relationship information often sits outside structured CRM fields. It can be in a management presentation attached to an opportunity, meeting notes on SharePoint, or a diligence file on a shared drive.
A professional may ask Claude about a deal without knowing that a relevant detail is in one of those documents. With a connection limited to CRM fields, that information is simply left out.
Navatar's enhanced Salesforce MCP brings that document information into the context used for the work. Users don't have to start by asking Claude to summarize a particular file. Relevant content can inform the response or supported activity alongside information already in the CRM.
Document access becomes a way to account for information the user didn't know to ask for, not just a tool for examining a file they have already found.
Context From Documents Across Connected Systems
Supported sources include:
Documents stored within Navatar CRM.
SharePoint.
Other connected document management systems.
Shared drives.
Firms don't have to move documents into a single repository before Claude can use them. Relevant information can be considered where it already resides, subject to the firm's supported connections, configuration, and access permissions.
Document Context in Every Claude Workflow
The document capabilities apply across the ways professionals already work with Claude and Navatar:
Working in Claude: Through Navatar's bidirectional Salesforce MCP connectivity, professionals can retrieve CRM information, develop research, and bring selected outcomes and supported actions back into Navatar. Relevant document information now informs that work too.
Working inside Navatar: Claude can suggest actions for users to consider, and actions users start can be routed through Claude with results returned to Navatar. Those suggestions and results can now reflect relevant document information as well as CRM records.
Whether work starts in Claude or in Navatar, it can draw on a more complete picture of the deal or relationship.

ExxonMobil (XOM +1.36%), Shell (SHEL +0.61%), and Chevron (CVX +0.97%) have their fingers on the pulse of the global energy market. However, energy is a commodity, so the best these integrated energy giants can do is react to what is taking place around them. Right now, with energy prices high, that's leading to strong financial results.
However, the key issue is the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East. This highly uncertain event has upended global energy markets, leaving energy companies and entire countries in flux. Here's what Exxon, Shell, and Chevron were thinking about when they discussed earnings. The big picture: Be prepared for continued uncertainty.
Exxon is clear about where the problem lies

Given that backdrop, it makes complete sense that balance sheet strength remains important. Novo Nordisk (NVO +0.96%) received a vote of confidence from JPMorgan Chase's (JPM +0.39%) analyst ahead of the drug maker's earnings report. The analyst was expecting strong Wegovy pill sales, and Novo Nordisk lived up to that expectation, having now racked up more than eight million cumulative prescriptions since the GLP-1 pill's launch. But is that enough to make the stock a buy? Here's how you can decide.
Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 pill is doing very well
Novo Nordisk was the first to market with a GLP-1 weight-loss shot, effectively creating a new drug category. And the opportunity is massive, given the prevalence of obesity worldwide. However, people don't really like to take shots. So it was important that Novo Nordisk was also the first to market with a GLP-1 pill. The launch of the Wegovy pill has been even more successful than the launch of the company's Wegovy shot.
That's great news, but investors have to view it within the context of the company's broader business plan. That's highlighted by the fact that Novo Nordisk's operating profit fell 9% year over year in the quarter. This wasn't a surprise; it was part of the plan. Novo Nordisk is using the pill launch to shift toward a high-volume/low-price model.
NVO Novo Nordisk

Right now, the low-price piece of the puzzle is depressing revenues and earnings. That's happening despite strong adoption of the Wegovy pill in what the company is calling a transition year. Strong results for the Wegovy pill hint that the plan is working, but the success of the plan won't be fully clear until the company's profits start to respond as well. And it is important to remember that Novo Nordisk doesn't operate in a vacuum. Key competitor Eli Lilly (LLY +0.35%) already has its own GLP-1 pill on the market, and additional competitors are waiting in the wings with their own GLP-1 drugs as well.
Novo Nordisk: A solid risk/reward balance
Thus, truly conservative investors may want to wait for more evidence. But Novo Nordisk's stock has fallen 70% from its 2024 peak. The 4.4% dividend yield is well above the pharmaceutical average of around 1.3% and backed by a strong 33% payout ratio. The stock's price-to-sales, price-to-earnings, and price-to-book ratios are all below their five-year averages. If you are an income and/or value investor, the stock looks attractive right now. The U.K. economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, in line with estimates, driven by output in the services sector.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected the economy to grow 0.7% from the previous quarter.
The economy grew 1.9% year-on-year in the three months to September.
The figures showed a slight improvement from the previous quarter, when gross domestic product grew by 0.5%. In the first quarter, the economy grew by 0.6%.
Services sector growth
The services sector expanded by 0.9%, data from the U.K.'s Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed on Thursday morning. It offset 0.1% output growth in the production sector and a 0.7% contraction in construction.
Within the services sector, information and communication was a key driver of growth, expanding by 2.1% in the quarter.
"This industry has been the largest driver of GDP growth across 2026, with evidence that many of the businesses reporting the largest increases in turnover are involved in activities related to artificial intelligence and cloud computing," the ONS said.
"However, because of the nature of our data collection, it is difficult for us to quantify the exact impact of these types of activities on turnover."
In September, the economy grew by 0.2% month-on-month, beating expectations that GDP would flatline. It marked an improvement from the previous month, with revised figures showing the British economy carved out zero growth in August.
U.K. finance minister John Healey said in a statement that the country was showing "stand-out resilience" despite the U.S.-Iran war hitting growth worldwide.
"Our U.K. economy is growing at the fastest rate in almost ten years, outside the pandemic," he said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the third-quarter growth was "bringing hope for the future."
The British pound was down by 0.2% against the U.S. dollar and flat against the euro on Thursday morning. Yields on U.K. government bonds were little changed.
Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, called the update a "decent set of results with the UK economy still proving to be relatively resilient since the US-Iran war started."
But he added that the economy's strength will be tested in the months ahead.
"Nervousness in the lead up to the Autumn Budget and continued uncertainty from the Middle East war is expected to weigh on confidence and activity over the coming GDP readings," he said in a note.
"With some already trimming their growth forecasts for next year, the U.K. economy still faces several headwinds."
AI provides 'an extra engine of growth'

Marsh & McLennan Cos. is urging US regulators to allow banks to hold less capital against loans covered by credit risk insurance as they look for new ways to offload data center exposure.
Demand for hedging AI-related finance has exploded, but US lenders have traditionally leaned more heavily on other instruments because insurance doesn’t free up regulatory capital for them, according Azi Larsen, a managing director in the credit specialties practice at the world’s biggest insurance broker.
“We’ve been doing a lot of advocacy around that in the US,” Larsen said in an interview with Bloomberg News. “Hopefully we’ll have a positive answer from the US regulators at the end of the year,” she added.
The Federal Reserve is set to complete its latest regulatory capital rules in the coming weeks, Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said at an event on Nov 10. The package is expected to include a plan that would lower the capital surcharge for the biggest US lenders and another that would change risk-based capital requirements for midsize and large banks.
Credit risk insurance has long been used by European banks to mitigate losses and release capital that can then be used to issue more loans. Lenders pay premiums to cover a percentage of losses on specific facilities. Barclays Plc has been looking to buy cover on more than $10 billion of data center debt, while HSBC Holdings Plc has explored a similar transaction.
With global spending on data centers projected by McKinsey & Co to hit $6.7 trillion by 2030, debt financing is expected to play a much bigger role, and finding different tools to manage risks has become “mission critical” for lenders, Larsen said.
Marsh is active in arranging credit risk insurance for project finance, including deals related to data centers. Despite its limitations, US lenders are increasingly turning to the product to cap their exposure to certain borrowers or industries as the volume of AI-related lending balloons.
“Even if they don’t get capital relief, they still see value in trying to use it,” Larsen added.

SpaceX must face a lawsuit accusing it of illegally firing eight engineers who raised concerns about alleged sexual harassment and discrimination at the company after a US appeals court on Tuesday rejected its request to send the case to private arbitration.
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a federal judge’s ruling that the engineers’ claims were exempt from the arbitration agreements they signed at SpaceX and can continue in court.
Spokespeople for SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the decision. SpaceX has denied the allegations.
The engineers’ attorney, Laurie Burgess, said they were “delighted” with the court’s “well-reasoned” decision. The engineers filed the lawsuit in 2024, claiming SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered their firing after they circulated a letter calling the billionaire a “distraction and embarrassment” and urging executives to disavow sexually charged comments he made on social media.
The lawsuit said Musk’s conduct fostered a “pervasively sexist culture” at SpaceX where female engineers were routinely subjected to harassment and sexist comments.
The 9th Circuit on Tuesday rejected SpaceX’s argument that the claims were not covered by a federal law that allows individuals to pursue lawsuits in “sexual harassment disputes” regardless of arbitration agreements.

Five US states have joined the Federal Trade Commission in a lawsuit that alleges telehealth company Hims & Hers Health engaged in deceptive and unlawful privacy practices, the FTC said on Oct. 10.
The lawsuit alleges the company shared consumers’ sensitive health information with third-party advertising platforms including Meta Platforms and Snap, despite claiming its services maintain consumers’ privacy.

Los Angeles County and Utah joined the action when the FTC initiated it in July.
Hims & Hers is one of the largest telehealth players in the market for weight-loss drugs. It also treats erectile dysfunction, hair loss and mental health conditions, shipping prescriptions directly to customers.
“We will vigorously defend ourselves against these follow-on claims, which rely on the same flawed allegations advanced in the government’s lawsuit,” a Hims & Hers spokesperson said.

Tech companies WiseTech and Atlassian have cut jobs this year, attributing the losses to AI. Telecommunications firm Telstra has also cut jobs from an AI joint venture with Accenture, with some work offshored to India.

A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight made an emergency landing on Tuesday at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble.
Two people were aboard the Bell 206L-4 helicopter when it came down on a road at the Port Jersey Marine Terminal in Bayonne, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, around 8:55 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
No injuries were reported, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said. Messages seeking comment were left for the helicopter’s operator, FlyNYON.
Video of the scene shows part of the helicopter’s tail sitting on the road about 30 feet (9 meters) from the aircraft, which was manufactured in 1999, according to FAA records.
In a recording of the air traffic control audio posted on the ATC app, the pilot can be heard saying, “Mayday, mayday, mayday” and “We need to land outside of the airport.” The helicopter landed several minutes later, just outside of the container terminal, the Port Authority said.
Last year, a Bell 206L-4 sightseeing helicopter plummeted into the Hudson River, killing all 6 people on board. The National Transportation Safety Board said the remains of several geese were found on the helicopter, suggesting it may have struck several birds before crashing.
NYC Helicopter Crash Prompts Push for New Tourist-Flight Rules
Last week, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General announced an audit of sightseeing helicopter regulations, citing “longstanding concerns regarding the industry’s safety and whether the current regulatory framework provides adequate safeguards.”
Since 2008, there have been at least 58 helicopter crashes involving tourist helicopters in the U.S., including 11 that were fatal, Assistant Inspector General Marshall Jackson said.

The tally of losses from the historic wildfires in Washington over the summer continues to grow, but by so do the lessons being learned.
Insured losses from the wildfires that plagued Washington for nearly half the summer are nearing $1 billion from roughly 3,500 claims, far exceeding projections of $600 million in September for what has become the most expensive wildfires in state history.
Those figures encompass all wildfires in the state from June to present, but most losses are from the Spokane Complex Fire, comprised of the Old Trails, Fairview and Autumn Lane fires that destroyed roughly 900 structures. An analysis from property data provider Cotality identified 5,256 properties that sustained at least some damage, of which 96% were single-family residences.
The fires, which ignited on Aug. 1, grew to 10,000-acres-plus, burned 19 days and prompted evacuations of more than 65,000 people.
The biggest insured loss came from the Old Trails Fire, which occurred in the wildland-urban interface, with an estimated $665 million in insured losses.
The blaze was studied by the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety researchers, who looked into how factors such as structure spacing, connective fuels and building components interact under the fire weather conditions.
The IBHS research on the Old Trails Fire in Spokane County, which destroyed 615 structures, shows connective fuels like combustible fences and mulch created pathways for fire to reach homes.
Researchers documented damage and fire-spread pathways at 132 structures across nine areas, identifying vulnerabilities involving windows, decks, building materials and other structural features.
Aerial imagery captured just six hours after ignition showed multiple fire outbreaks burning simultaneously. That stretched firefighting resources and left crews unable to protect all the threatened structures, according to the report.
“As a result, structures with vulnerabilities to ember exposure, including combustible roofs, unmitigated vents, or fuels directly adjacent to the home, remain(ed) at risk of ignition,” the IBHS report states. “This scenario led to significant losses within the perimeter, even after the advancing fire front had slowed, and illustrates the challenges of structure protection, fire suppression, and fire management in communities with vulnerable structures.”
Researchers looked at the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires to compare the distances between the structures in the Eaton Fire with structural distances in the Old Trails Fire. They concluded the Washington fire could have been worse had the housing density been greater.
They found that most (58%) structures in the Eaton Fire had another structure within 10 feet, while only 13.8% of structures within the Old Trails Fire perimeter were spaced so closely.
Fire-resistant building materials alone were not always enough to keep a home safe. Researchers identified instances in which combustible landscaping allowed flames to reach fire-resistant exterior walls.
In one case, burning mulch ignited combustible components beneath noncombustible lap siding where a wall met the foundation. Reported ties between Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI powerhouse Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy have sparked an investigation by the FBI, calls for congressional hearings, a review by the company’s independent directors and a proposed investor class action lawsuit.
Below is a look at the potential legal exposure for Huang, Nvidia NVDA.O and the directors of the company, which dominates the global market for computer chips that power the AI economy.
WHAT ARE THE ALLEGATIONS?
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, whom US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed has faced US scrutiny over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips whose export to China is restricted.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s Huang admitted he was unfaithful to his wife without providing details about the relationship, which led to a drop in Nvidia’s stock price. Trump said Huang told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy and Huang has not been accused of criminal wrongdoing.
Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation, which China’s foreign ministry has said was “groundless,” nor has it verified Alice Huang’s current employment status with Megaspeed.
Nvidia has said its board has “no reason to believe” US national security or company secrets were affected, though an independent committee of directors will review all available information. The company said on Tuesday the independent directors hired the Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz law firm to assist with its investigation.
Nvidia sits at the center of the technological rivalry between the United States and China. Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China since 2022. News of the affair has emerged as Democrats seized control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, propelled in part by anti-AI and anti-corruption sentiment.
WHAT ABOUT FEDERAL SECURITIES FRAUD?
A proposed class action was filed in San Jose, California, federal court on Monday alleging the company and Huang defrauded shareholders by concealing Huang’s alleged relationship. The proposed class would cover Nvidia investors who bought the stock between October 9, when Nvidia denied claims in a New York Times report about Megaspeed ties to China, and November 8, when the board announced its investigation and Huang acknowledged he had an affair. The period includes October 30, when Huang told Bloomberg Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed was “normal and not unusual.”
Securities fraud plaintiffs must show, among other things, that Nvidia and Huang knowingly misled investors, that investors relied on those misleading statements and that those misleading statements artificially inflated the stock.
The lawsuit did not specify damages but the stock lost around 20% during the class period, a decline of around $1 trillion in market value.
Such lawsuits are often filed in the wake of a company’s stock suffering a large drop, and more are likely.

It finally clicked for Jordan Walker.
Following a scorching start to his Major League career in 2023, the heralded Cardinals prospect slumped over the next two seasons.
Then it happened: Walker broke out with a performance commensurate with the lofty expectations. The 24-year-old right fielder hit 29 home runs, drove in 102 runs and stole 22 bases for St. Louis this past season, earning his first career All-Star selection. He even won the Home Run Derby in Philadelphia along the way, defeating heavyweight hometown favorite Kyle Schwarber.
And on Wednesday, it was announced at the MLB Awards presented by MGM Rewards that Walker had been selected to the All-MLB Second Team.

The All-MLB Team was established in 2019 to recognize baseball’s best players at each position based on regular-season play. The honor was introduced to highlight players’ full-season contributions, given that All-Star selections are based on first-half performance. Fans voted at MLB.com to help choose First and Second Team selections at each position (including three outfielders, a designated hitter, five starting pitchers and two relievers).
Walker’s first-half performance this year made him one of the best offensive players in the sport. At the All-Star break, his slash line was .294/.354/.532 and he had belted 22 homers. He continued to hit well through August, but struggled in September, when he posted a .519 OPS.
Walker’s overall performance was still a major step forward in a career that could feature more All-Star selections in the future.
In particular, Walker’s bat speed was elite -- his average bat speed of 79.3 mph was second only to AL MVP finalist Junior Caminero (79.4 mph). Walker also barreled the ball at a career-best rate of 13.2%. He cut his strikeout rate significantly, down to 26.1% last season after he struck out 31.8% of the time in 2025.
The results were the fruit of a simplified approach he worked on with his hitting coaches during the offseason.
Defensively, Walker’s arm was one of the best among outfielders -- his average arm strength of 96.5 mph ranked in the 99th percentile, according to Statcast.
With well-above-average sprint speed (29.1 feet per second on average), Walker swiped 22 bases in 27 attempts and produced +3 baserunning run value (87th percentile among qualified baserunners).
Walker’s Home Run Derby win made him the first Cardinals entrant to win the midsummer showcase. His victory was stunning given his final-round opponent, the venue in which he was taking aim at the bleachers and how calm and cool he was in his first Derby appearance.
In his final round, after Schwarber tallied 12 home runs to make Walker’s task a tall one -- especially with the biased crowd at Citizens Bank Park -- Walker deposited six straight over the fence to capture the Derby crown in dramatic fashion.
